pr_title: Issue 81523: do not ignore writable layer when on a device other than rootFS
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Writable layer ephemeral space consumption is ignored when the runtime imageFS is not on the Kubernetes root filesystem.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #81523

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**: Yes
```release-note
Depending upon node configuration, eviction for overconsumption of local ephemeral storage does not happen when the storage consumed is in the container writable layer (e. g. /tmp).  The conditions under which this does not work are that the runtime image storage (e. g. /var/lib/crio, /var/lib/docker) is not on the same filesystem device as the Kubernetes root filesystem.
```

**Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.**:

I'm slightly confused here.  Empty-dir volumes should always be on the rootfs, even when using a separate imagefs for container images and writable layers.

This is a problem with writable layers.

Maybe I need to open a new issue; somehow I thought the existing one involved writable layers.
It might.  The title of this PR is misleading if that is what it is fixing
/cc

> It might. The title of this PR is misleading if that is what it is fixing

The title was flat out wrong, and I've created issue #81523 for this.

"Ephemeral storage" refers only to the root filesystem, not to the image filesystem (if it exists).  IIRC, we made that decision early on in the ephemeral storage design because we didn't want to expose the implementation detail of 1 filesystem vs 2 to users.  When using two filesystems, the kubelet still does eviction when the imageFS runs low, but does not count container writable layer towards the pod's ephemeral storage usage.

> "Ephemeral storage" refers only to the root filesystem, not to the image filesystem (if it exists). IIRC, we made that decision early on in the ephemeral storage design because we didn't want to expose the implementation detail of 1 filesystem vs 2 to users. When using two filesystems, the kubelet still does eviction when the imageFS runs low, but does not count container writable layer towards the pod's ephemeral storage usage.

The problem is that it wasn't doing eviction if consumption of the writable layer exceeded the limit (verified on current master).  This created confusion on the part of a customer who expected that the ephemeral storage limit would limit what pods could write to ephemeral storage.  Having different behavior depending upon whether the image filesystem is on the root filesystem is confusing and does expose the implementation detail of 1 vs. 2 filesystems.

If it's behaving as expected, there does at a minimum need to be a comment in the code clearly explaining that it was a deliberate decision and why, but I think the current behavior is problematic.  Filling up the image filesystem is almost as serious as filling up the root filesystem, at least for container users.

> The problem is that it wasn't doing eviction if consumption of the writable layer exceeded the limit (verified on current master). This created confusion on the part of a customer who expected that the ephemeral storage limit would limit what pods could write to ephemeral storage. Having different behavior depending upon whether the image filesystem is on the root filesystem is confusing and does expose the implementation detail of 1 vs. 2 filesystems.

The public documentation for this is [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#local-ephemeral-storage).  That seems fairly clear: "If an optional runtime partition is used, root partition will not hold any image layer or writable layers."  If you have a better way to word this, feel free to open a PR to the website.  "Ephemeral Storage" refers specifically to the filesystem the kubelet is on.  So technically, the pod is not consuming ephemeral storage when writing to a container writable layer that isn't on the kubelet's filesystem.

It was incorrect for to say that we wanted to entirely hide the implementation detail of 1 vs 2 filesystems.  Obviously, it comes into play here when using two filesystems.  It would probably be more accurate to say that we thought that limiting the ephemeral storage feature to a single filesystem, rather than adding "Root Ephemeral Storage" vs "Image Ephemeral Storage" as two schedulable resources would be simpler for users to reason about, and would still allow us to provide better guarantees about ephemeral disk access.

> Filling up the image filesystem is almost as serious as filling up the root filesystem, at least for container users.

When the imagefs.available --eviction-hard parameter is set, the kubelet will still perform eviction when the imagefs fills up.  If this isn't working, then the kubelet either isn't correctly detecting the image fs, or doesn't have the correct eviction configuration for the image fs (or there is some other bug).  The Ephemeral Storage feature wasn't introduced to prevent the filesystem from filling up.  That was already accomplished by disk eviction.

> > The problem is that it wasn't doing eviction if consumption of the writable layer exceeded the limit (verified on current master). This created confusion on the part of a customer who expected that the ephemeral storage limit would limit what pods could write to ephemeral storage. Having different behavior depending upon whether the image filesystem is on the root filesystem is confusing and does expose the implementation detail of 1 vs. 2 filesystems.
> 
> The public documentation for this is [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#local-ephemeral-storage). That seems fairly clear: "If an optional runtime partition is used, root partition will not hold any image layer or writable layers." If you have a better way to word this, feel free to open a PR to the website. "Ephemeral Storage" refers specifically to the filesystem the kubelet is on. So technically, the pod is not consuming ephemeral storage when writing to a container writable layer that isn't on the kubelet's filesystem.
> 
> It was incorrect for to say that we wanted to entirely hide the implementation detail of 1 vs 2 filesystems. Obviously, it comes into play here when using two filesystems. It would probably be more accurate to say that we thought that limiting the ephemeral storage feature to a single filesystem, rather than adding "Root Ephemeral Storage" vs "Image Ephemeral Storage" as two schedulable resources would be simpler for users to reason about, and would still allow us to provide better guarantees about ephemeral disk access.

> 
> When the imagefs.available --eviction-hard parameter is set, the kubelet will still perform eviction when the imagefs fills up. If this isn't working, then the kubelet either isn't correctly detecting the image fs, or doesn't have the correct eviction configuration for the image fs (or there is some other bug). The Ephemeral Storage feature wasn't introduced to prevent the filesystem from filling up. That was already accomplished by disk eviction.

I see.  This seems counter-intuitive to me, as it means that consumption of this shared space on a per-pod basis can only be performed if the imagefs is on the root filesystem.

[monitoring-ephemeral-storage-consumption](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#monitoring-ephemeral-storage-consumption) says: 

>The monitoring is performed by scanning each emptyDir volume, log directories, and *writable layers* on a periodic basis.

At least for me, it means *writable layers* is part of the ephemeral storage consumption by a Pod, independent of where writable layer resides in. (e.g whether has a separate image fs or not).

[how-pods-with-ephemeral-storage-limits-run](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/#how-pods-with-ephemeral-storage-limits-run) says:
>For container-level isolation, if a Container’s writable layer and logs usage exceeds its storage limit, the Pod will be evicted.

But in current implementation, the limit for ephemeral storage  will exhibit different behaviour depend on whether there is separate imagefs partition or not. This is a surprise for user.

>Ephemeral Storage" refers specifically to the filesystem the kubelet is on. 

It will be good to make it explicit to say explicitly that the separate imagefs don't count in as Ephemeral stroage and thus the writable layer won't counted when enforcing the Ephemeral storage limit.

> The monitoring is performed by scanning each emptyDir volume, log directories, and writable layers on a periodic basis.

Yeah, that is more a description of disk space monitoring in general.  We still monitor all of those things, they are just not all always on the ephemeral storage filesystem.

> > The monitoring is performed by scanning each emptyDir volume, log directories, and writable layers on a periodic basis.
> 
> Yeah, that is more a description of disk space monitoring in general. We still monitor all of those things, they are just not all always on the ephemeral storage filesystem.

@dashpole  

A little bit off-topic but related question: How the statistic of writeable layer of the a container is gathered? Does kubelet get it from cAdvisor? 

I met an issue the ephemeral storage limit is not working even the imagefs is on the root partition. 

I deployed a container "tinytool" in a Pod "busybox-sleep" into namespace "bar" with the ephemeral storage limit set as 50M but was able to create 100M file in that container without it being killed (more for 60minutes, the housekeeping interval is 20m). My hypothesis now is the kubelet eviction manager won't be able to get the correct stats from cAdvisor to perform the eviction but can't prove it. 

I assume following command will give the stats of the container in question, but it gave me an internal error:
```
curl -k --cert cert.pem --key key.pem https://localhost:10250/stats/bar/busybox-sleep/5d3af380-c3d3-11e9-b5cd-20677cde3e90/tinytool
Internal Error: unable to find docker container "fdc6347cde9d5142cc4f89a4150100b9efbca0d2c2d3c3b3367b2482f562b12a" 
```
while `docker inspect fdc6347c` will show the exactly container (`tinytool`) I'm trying to debug.

Would you mind sharing where I should look at the issue? Thank you.

Sorry for hijacking the thread. @RobertKrawitz

> > The monitoring is performed by scanning each emptyDir volume, log directories, and writable layers on a periodic basis.
> 
> Yeah, that is more a description of disk space monitoring in general. We still monitor all of those things, they are just not all always on the ephemeral storage filesystem.

It's more specific than that:

>  For container-level isolation, **if a Container’s _writable layer_ and logs usage exceeds its storage limit, the Pod will be evicted**. For pod-level isolation, if the sum of the local ephemeral storage usage from all containers and also the Pod’s emptyDir volumes exceeds the limit, the Pod will be evicted.

While that doesn't explicitly call out writable layers for pod-level isolation, it does for container isolation, and as written it appears inclusive of container utilization, including writable layer (my highlight).

From the standpoint of a user or system administrator, it would appear very strange to me that an overall limit might or might not apply depending upon exactly how the underlying system (not visible from the pod) were configured.  In the case of a home directory, of course, a quota (either project or user/group) does apply only to that directory or filesystem, but it's transparent that, say, /tmp is not the same as a home directory.

As it stands, someone might develop an application, including pod definitions, on a cluster that happens to separate root and imagefs, and the application would succeed despite the limit being exceeded.  When run on a different system with a combined root and imagefs, the application would fail with the pod's eviction.  The application developer, attempting to reproduce the problem, would not succeed in doing so for a reason that is not at all obvious (as was the case for me investigating the customer-reported bug that led to my opening this PR).

My concern with this issue is that it can be exploited, intentionally or unintentionally, as a denial of service against the kubelet.

If you fill the imagefs and kubernetes can't act on it, you effectively block the node from functioning on anything that requires space for images or, more importantly, existing pods which need space for the writable layer.

This is definitely worth discussing and addressing even if it was outside the original scope.

> My concern with this issue is that it can be exploited, intentionally or unintentionally, as a denial of service against the kubelet.  If you fill the imagefs and kubernetes can't act on it, you effectively block the node from functioning on anything that requires space for images or, more importantly, existing pods which need space for the writable layer.

It would be bad if this issue prevented the node from functioning, but isn't what this issue is about.  The mechanism for addressing that problem is imagefs disk eviction, and was added in v1.4.  This is about the ephemeral storage feature, which allows pods to set requests and limits for disk.

I think it is clear that this behavior is confusing when using multiple filesystems.  I just haven't found a better solution.

If we were to count the imagefs as ephemeral storage as well, we end up with scheduling problems.  E.g. if the imagefs and rootfs are both 10Gi, the node reports 20Gi of capacity/allocatable.  But if I try and run a pod that writes a 15Gi file to either its writable layer or to an empty-dir volume, it will run out of space.

We could count the imagefs as ephemeral storage, but only for the purpose of enforcing limits.  I.E. Capacity/Allocatable are based on the capacity of the rootfs, and requests are counted against that.  If we did that, we would end up with two different numbers for "usage", which would be confusing for users.  One would be "usage" of requests, which would be only usage on the rootfs, and would be used during out-of-resource eviction ranking.  The other would be all usage, which would be usage of the rootfs and imagefs, and would be compared with the limits when enforcing them.

The option we did consider initially is having two separate resources for disk: one for the rootfs, and another for the image fs.  This way everything is consistent.  Each resource has its own capacity, allocatable, requests, limits, and usage.  We decided against this because of the complexity it forced to users, and opted to only scope the Ephemeral Storage feature to the rootfs.  We accepted that the feature wouldn't work perfectly with a separate imagefs, but didn't think the additional complexity was worth it.

Let me know if you can think of a better solution.

issue_context.title: When runtime imagefs mount is not on root filesystem, writable layer usage does not count toward ephemeral storage consumption
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**: When the writable layer of a pod is not on the Kubernetes root filesystem (e. g. /var/lib/crio or /var/lib/docker is not on the Kubernetes root filesystem), it's possible to create an arbitrary amount of data without triggering eviction based on ephemeral storage limit

**What you expected to happen**: When creating 1GB of data in /tmp on a pod whose ephemeral-storage limit is 1MB, it should be evicted.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

1) Ensure that /var/lib/crio or /var/lib/docker is on a different filesystem from the Kubernetes root.
2) Run the following pod:

```apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
max:
metadata:
  name: "failpod"
spec:
  containers:
  - name: "failpod"
    image: "busybox"
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: "100Ki"
    command:
      - /bin/sh
      - -c
      - |
        dd if=/dev/zero of='/tmp/test.file' bs=1024 count='1000'
        sleep infinity
```

**Anything else we need to know?**: Fix is in PR 81516

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): Any since late 2017
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): N/A
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): N/A
- Install tools: N/A
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug): N/A
- Others: N/A

review_comments: Out of curiosity, do you know why we had this conditional in the first place?

No I don't, and I'm a bit concerned about that.  I attempted to contact the author of this code (it appears to have been introduced about 2 years ago as part of another change, but with no explanation in the code or commit comment), but my email bounced.  Given the way this is used it's not apparent to me why there would be any reason for this kind of check in this place, although I could see it being useful elsewhere.
